guest: A guest orders ramen and says they might like something else, but they are not sure what.
q: What is the best way to continue?
choices: Ask what kind of food or experience they are in the mood for, then suggest a verified menu option
Immediately name the most expensive appetizer
List several random items until one sounds appealing
Tell them every ramen order needs a side
why: Start with the guest's preferences. Then make one relevant recommendation you can accurately describe.

guest: A guest says, “No thanks, I’m good with what I ordered.”
choices: Respect the decision and move on
Offer the same item again later
Tell them they are missing out
Suggest a more expensive alternative
why: A good recommendation is an offer, not pressure. Respecting a decline is part of good service.

guest: A guest says they are trying to keep the meal within a specific budget.
q: Which response best supports the guest?
choices: Ignore the budget and recommend a premium item
Ask what range they have in mind and suggest an appropriate confirmed option
Tell them the budget is too low
Add an item without asking
why: Treat the budget as a real preference. Offer an option that fits and make the price clear.

guest: A guest asks whether an appetizer contains an allergen. You do not know the full ingredients or preparation details.
choices: Guess from the menu description
Say it is probably safe
Pause the recommendation and verify with the kitchen using allergen procedures
Suggest they try a small amount
why: Allergen questions are not upselling opportunities. Accuracy and safety come first; never guess or suggest testing an allergen.

guest: A guest asks what you would pair with their order. You are unsure which combinations the restaurant recommends.
choices: Invent a pairing that sounds good
Check the approved recommendations or ask an experienced team member before suggesting an item
Recommend the most expensive item by default
Say every item pairs well with everything
why: Only recommend pairings you can support with accurate menu knowledge. If unsure, check before presenting it as a recommendation.
